name: Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Homestead
aka: the American Fur Company factory building
the Beaubien house on the reservation

documented_range.note:
THE RANGE IS WIDE BECAUSE THE BUILDING IS OLD, NOT BECAUSE THE RESEARCH IS THIN, and the project's own gate warns about ranges this long so the reason is stated here. Andreas: the building was the American Fur Company's factory building, erected by Capt. Bradley, and Jean Baptiste Beaubien bought it in 1817. No month is given, so the range opens at the start of that year. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS BETTER ATTESTED THAN ON MOST RECORDS IN THIS DATASET: Beaubien was living on the reservation in 1835 and filed a pre-emption claim for the whole 75.69-acre fort reservation dated 28 May 1835 and recorded 26 June 1835 at $94.61 — five weeks old on the scene date — and the Chicago Historical Society's later plaque still placed the homestead on the block that became the Public Library. What is NOT attested is the date the building came down, so 1835-12-31 is a housekeeping bound at the end of the scene year and not a demolition date. The claim was voided by the Supreme Court in Wilcox v. Jackson in 1839, which is four years after this scene and outside it.

ADDED 2026-09-06 UNDER T-0718, AND IT IS A CORRECTION TO THE SENTENCE ABOVE RATHER THAN AN ADDITION TO IT. Two further Andreas pages were read off the scan while settling the corner, and together they show that the '1817' in this range — and in this phase's id — FUSES TWO DIFFERENT BUILDINGS. Scan p. 183: 'In 1815, a short time before the rebuilding of the fort, an army contractor named Dean, built a house on the lake shore, at the mouth of the Chicago River, near where is now the foot of Randolph Street. In 1817, Mr. Beaubien purchased this house, which was a low, gloomy building of five rooms, for $1,000 ... After this purchase he lived in the Dean house for several years'. Scan p. 205: 'In 1822, after the abandonment of the United States Factory at Chicago, by Government, the factory building was bought by the American Fur Company, and soon after sold to John B. Beaubien, who made it his dwelling house.' SO THE 1817 PURCHASE WAS OF THE DEAN HOUSE AT THE LAKE SHORE, AND THE FACTORY BUILDING CAME TO BEAUBIEN IN 1822 — which is the year and the chain `bk_afc_009` gives, so Andreas and Hurlbut's Hubbard AGREE about the factory building and the disagreement this record used to report between them was an artefact of the conflation. NOTHING IS MOVED ON THIS TICKET: changing the bound renames the phase, and with it the committed GLB, two manifests, the 1835 sidecar and a docs/LIBERTIES.md coverage line, which is more than this ticket's demonstration. The bound stands as a floor — the building this record models is OLDER than 1817 on either reading — and the correction is carried by T-0893. The 'erected by Capt. Bradley' attribution above could not be relocated on any of the four pages read here; the source record warns that the archive.org index is lossy, so that is 'not found', not 'not present'.

position.symbolic_location: On the Fort Dearborn reservation at what Andreas calls the corner of South Water Street and Michigan Avenue (today East Wacker Drive at North Michigan Avenue) — the NORTH-EAST corner, which is the side of Michigan Avenue the 1839 sale of this homestead was on.
position.note:
PLACED 2026-08-11 ON THE SOUTH-WEST CORNER; MOVED TO THE NORTH-EAST 2026-09-06 UNDER T-0718, AFTER THE TWO PASSAGES THE OLD ARGUMENT WEIGHED AGAINST EACH OTHER WERE READ DIRECTLY OFF THE SCAN RATHER THAN AT SECOND HAND. The move is about 47 m north-east. Confidence stays `inferred` and the working uncertainty is unchanged: a better-argued corner is still a retrospective corner.

WHAT THE OLD ARGUMENT SAID, AND WHY IT DOES NOT SURVIVE THE READING. It adopted the south-west on the ground that Andreas scan p. 185 is a statement ABOUT the homestead while scan p. 339 uses the corner as a waypoint in a boundary walk through Block 5, and that a statement about the thing outranks a statement that passes it. The rule is right. The reading of p. 339 was wrong. P. 339 IS NOT A BOUNDARY WALK AND IT IS NOT ANDREAS: it is John Wentworth's address of 21 May 1881, reprinted, and the sentence is an instruction for finding this house. Verbatim off the scan (archive.org historyofchicago01andr, scan p. 339): 'If you wish to find the traditional residence of General Jean Baptiste Beaubien, after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house, go east upon South Water Street until you come to the northeast corner of South Water Street and Michigan Avenue, and you will find it.' Applied honestly, the old rule now points at the north-east: p. 339 is the passage that is about the building.

ONE WITNESS, NOT TWO. That sentence is word for word the sentence `chicagology_prefire052` reprints and `wentworth_1881_fort_dearborn` holds as a document, so Andreas p. 339 and Wentworth are ONE witness reaching this project twice — Andreas 1884 carrying Wentworth 1881. This does not weaken the reading; it identifies it, and it is written here so that no later run counts the north-east twice.

THE SOUTH-WEST SENTENCE CITES THE TRANSACTION THAT CONTRADICTS IT. Andreas scan p. 185, read directly: 'The homestead of Colonel Beaubien was where now is the southwest corner of South Water Street and Michigan Avenue. This was bid in at the land sale in June, 1839, by James H. Collins, for $1,049.' The sale it names is the one Wentworth narrates on p. 339 — same buyer, same price — and Wentworth says which land it was: 'the land upon the east side of Michigan Avenue, in Block 5, between South Water Street and the lots reserved, where the Marine Hospital afterward was, except the corner lot, known as Lot 11 ... Mr. Collins bid $1,049 for the next five lots, 10, 9, 8, 7, and 6, where Beaubien's house, out-buildings, and garden were.' East side of Michigan Avenue, north of South Water Street, south of the reserved lots: that is the north-east quadrant, and it is the only quadrant of the four the sale can have been in. So p. 185's second clause places the ground its first clause mis-sites, and the south-west now rests on a single word inside a sentence that argues against it.

WHAT IS STILL NOT KNOWN, AND WHY THE CORNER IS TAKEN AS THE INSTRUCTION GIVES IT. Wentworth's own lot list puts the house, out-buildings and garden on lots 6 to 10 — the five lots NORTH of corner lot 11, which Beaubien kept — so the buildings stood some distance north of the corner itself and 'go until you come to the north-east corner and you will find it' is the finder's approximation, not a survey. No plat of the Fort Dearborn Addition carrying a lot dimension for Block 5 has been read by this project, so that distance is not quantified and is not invented here. The committed point is therefore a floor: the true position is at the corner or NORTH of it, never south or west of it.

THE CAVEAT THAT STILL MATTERS MORE THAN THE CORNER, UNCHANGED. NEITHER STREET EXISTED HERE IN 1835. The reservation was unplatted, no street crossed it, and South Water Street was ordered pitched only 'from the United States Reservation to Randolph Street'. Wentworth is speaking in 1881 and Andreas writing in 1884, both locating an old building by the streets of their own day, and the Fort Dearborn Addition whose Block 5 they cite was not platted until 1839. 'The corner of South Water and Michigan' is a retrospective locator and not an address this building ever had; any future evidence should be read as fixing it relative to the FORT, not to a grid that arrived later.

METHOD, THE MIRROR OF THE OLD ONE SO THE TWO ARE COMPARABLE. The modern East Upper Wacker Drive / North Michigan Avenue intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 448187.6, N 4637558.4 (four nodes averaged, spread 18.3 m, fetched 2026-08-11). The south-west placement put the origin 12.2 m west and 12.2 m south of that centre less the building's own width and depth; this one puts it 12.2 m EAST and 12.2 m NORTH of the same centre, so the footprint sits in the north-east quadrant with the same clearance from the retrospective kerb lines. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for the retrospective locator itself, plus the unmeasured northward offset above. The 45 m the two corners disagreed by is no longer an uncertainty on this record; it is a decided question, and the decision is written above rather than averaged away.

GROUND. The point stands on traced ground in the e1834_harbor_cut heightfield at +3.48 m above the summer-1835 water surface, against +2.51 m where it stood before — it has moved up the sand ridge east of the fort rather than off it, and the south bank of the main stem at this easting lies about 70 m further north again. Facade bearing 0 is unchanged, north toward the river, and it still has NO attested basis whatever: the streets it would face did not exist, and the bearing is a placeholder inherited from the retrospective grid.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module and the 2026-09-06 move did not create one: the input is a sentence in an 1881 address, not a measurable. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note.

footprint.note: INVENTED. No source reached gives the factory building a dimension. 12.192 x 6.096 m is 40 x 20 ft, and both numbers are borrowed from attested buildings in this dataset rather than freshly guessed: 20 ft is the depth of Hogan's store, the one log footprint here that is documented, and 40 ft is the frontage attested for the Green Tree Tavern. A fur company's factory building is a trade house — a store room and a counter — so a long shallow rectangle of that order is the right kind of shape for the type. THIS POLYGON IS ONE BUILDING AND THE HOMESTEAD WAS FOUR. Andreas describes the factory building bought in 1817, a new residence Beaubien built, a small trading post, and an earlier cabin he converted to a barn. Only the factory building is modelled; the other three are recorded in this record's research_note and in docs/RESEARCH/jb_beaubien_homestead.md and are not built.

construction.note: NOT STATED BY ANY SOURCE REACHED. Log is the reading from date and place: this is a building erected at Chicago before 1817, when the only other structures on the ground were Fort Dearborn's own and a handful of traders' houses, and this project's dossier records the settlement's stock as log until frame arrived with the town. Brick is excluded by the same dossier — no brick building of consequence on the south side before 1837. If the factory building was in fact frame, this record has the right massing on the wrong archetype and should move to a frame archetype rather than being repainted.

stories.note: LEFT AT 1 ON T-0718, DELIBERATELY, AGAINST A SOURCE THAT SAYS TWO — and the reason has changed even though the number has not. `bk_hub_063` (Hubbard, 1911, describing the place as he found it in 1818) calls the Factor House 'a two-story, squared-log structure, inclosed by a neat split-picket fence'. Until 2026-09-06 that was filed as irrelevant unless the identity in the research note went one way; the reading done on T-0718 makes the identity MORE likely, not less — Andreas scan p. 205 has the factory building sold on to Beaubien in 1822 'who made it his dwelling house', which is the same chain `bk_afc_009` gives, and Wentworth's 'traditional residence, after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house' is then that dwelling house. IT IS STILL NOT SETTLED, and the thing that blocks it is a POSITION, not a date: Andreas p. 191 and Hurlbut's Hubbard both put the factory building 'just south of the fort', and this record stands north of the fort on a corner two independent passages agree the homestead occupied. Doubling the massing of the oldest building in this dataset on a 1911 recollection of 1818, about a building whose own sources site it somewhere this record is not, is exactly the move the research note forbids. So: 1, inferred from the type and the date as before, with the two-storey reading named here rather than buried, and the identity carried by T-0894. If T-0894 settles the identity toward the Factor House, this value moves to 2 and the building is rebaked.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill. The same reading and the same number this project gives Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is this archetype's mid-range for a low single-storey log building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One is the minimum for a building lived in through Chicago winters and the archetype's default. The COUNT is the inference; the stack's position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

phases.change_note: The American Fur Company's factory building, erected by Capt. Bradley and bought by Jean Baptiste Beaubien in 1817 — the oldest structure this dataset models. By the scene date it is the principal building of a homestead group on the Fort Dearborn reservation, and Beaubien's pre-emption claim to the whole reservation is five weeks old: dated 28 May 1835, recorded 26 June 1835.

function.note: The building's original function is documented — a fur company factory, that is, a trade house. Its function on the scene date is the inference: Andreas has Beaubien building a NEW residence and a small trading post alongside it, which implies the old factory building had been superseded in at least one of those roles by 1835 without saying which. Recorded as both because nothing says it stopped being either.

occupants.value: Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien and his household
occupants.note: Beaubien is documented as the owner from 1817 and as the reservation's claimant in 1835. WHICH BUILDING OF THE HOMESTEAD GROUP HE ACTUALLY SLEPT IN ON THE SCENE DATE IS NOT ATTESTED — Andreas says he built a new residence, which is a different building from this one and is not modelled. Nothing further about the household is stated here; see review_required and the research note.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS 79 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.
land_owner.tract: the south-west fractional quarter of section 10

research_note: THE OLDEST BUILDING IN THIS DATASET AND THE LEAST PRECISELY PLACED. Three things are worth carrying out of this record. FIRST, THE CORNER IS DECIDED, AND IT WAS DECIDED THE OTHER WAY ON 2026-09-06 (T-0718). It used to read 'contested within Andreas himself — south-west on scan p. 185, north-east on scan p. 339' with the south-west adopted because p. 339 was believed to be a boundary walk. Both pages were then read directly off the scan. P. 339 is not a boundary walk and is not Andreas: it is John Wentworth's 1881 address reprinted, and its sentence is an instruction for finding this very house. P. 185's own second clause names the 1839 sale that Wentworth describes on p. 339 — same buyer, same $1,049 — and Wentworth says the land was 'upon the east side of Michigan Avenue, in Block 5, between South Water Street and the lots reserved'. The building moved about 47 m to the NORTH-EAST corner. Full argument in position.note; Andreas p. 339 and `wentworth_1881_fort_dearborn` are ONE witness, not two. SECOND, NEITHER STREET EXISTED THERE IN 1835: the reservation was unplatted and no street crossed it, so Andreas's corner is a retrospective locator, and any future evidence should be read as fixing the building relative to the FORT, not to a grid that arrived later. THIRD, THE HOMESTEAD WAS A GROUP AND ONLY ONE BUILDING OF IT IS MODELLED. Andreas records four elements: the American Fur Company factory building bought in 1817 (this record), a new residence Beaubien built, a small trading post, and an earlier cabin converted to a barn. The other three are attested and unbuilt, and the reason is that nothing reached gives any of them a size, a material, a form or a position relative to the factory building — they would be three invented boxes placed by eye around a fourth. A LIVE FACT FOR THE SCENE: Beaubien's pre-emption certificate for the entire 75.69-acre fort reservation is dated 28 May 1835 and was recorded 26 June 1835 at $94.61, so on 1835-07-01 it is five weeks old and unchallenged. It was voided by Wilcox v. Jackson in 1839. REVIEW IS FLAGGED ON THIS RECORD DELIBERATELY, for the reason given in madore_beaubien_house: AGENTS.md's standing constraint holds that Native presence and representation require consultation rather than inference, the final removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago falls in August 1835 weeks after this scene, and the Beaubien family's history runs directly into both that and the reservation claim. This record states built fabric and the documented dates of the claim, and leaves interpretation to a review this project has not yet sought. See docs/RESEARCH/jb_beaubien_homestead.md. FOURTH, THE ORIGIN AND THE JOHN DEAN QUESTION — OPENED 2026-09-04 (T-0595) AND ANSWERED 2026-09-06 (T-0718). The question was: Hubbard names JOHN DEAN as the United States factor who succeeded Jouett at the Factor House (`bk_hub_063`), and Wentworth finds Beaubien's residence 'after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house' — so if the two John Deans were one man, Beaubien had LEFT the Factory House and this record modelled the house he moved TO. THE PREMISE DOES NOT SURVIVE THE READING, and it fails on the HOUSE rather than on the man. Andreas scan p. 183: an army contractor NAMED DEAN built a house in 1815 'on the lake shore, at the mouth of the Chicago River, near where is now the foot of Randolph Street', 'a low, gloomy building of five rooms', and Beaubien bought THAT house in 1817 for $1,000 and lived in it 'for several years'. Andreas scan p. 191 then keeps the two apart in a single paragraph: Varnum 'boarded in the old John Dean house, with J. B. Beaubien, then its owner', while 'the building, which was just south of the fort' — the factory — went to Whiting, to the American Fur Company, and to Beaubien. THE JOHN-DEAN HOUSE IS THEREFORE A THIRD BUILDING, not the Factor House: a lakeshore house at the foot of Randolph Street with its own builder, date, price and room count. Whether Andreas's contractor Dean and Hubbard's factor John Dean are ONE MAN IS NOT ESTABLISHED, in as many words — Andreas supplies the forename 'John' for the house and Hubbard the office for the man, and no source reached joins them — but it no longer matters to this record, because the sentence turns on which HOUSE Beaubien left, and Andreas answers that directly. Read forward, the sequence is: the Dean house at the lake shore from 1817; the factory building from 1822 (Andreas p. 205 and `bk_afc_009`, agreeing); and Wentworth's 'traditional residence, after he moved from ... the John-Dean house' is that second building, at the corner this record now stands on. SO THIS RECORD IS MORE LIKELY THE FACTORY HOUSE THAN IT WAS, AND STILL NOT PROVED TO BE IT: Andreas p. 191 and Hurlbut's Hubbard both put the factory building JUST SOUTH OF THE FORT, and this record stands north of it. That contradiction is the whole of what is left of the question, and it is filed as T-0894 rather than resolved by preferring the source that agrees with the position already committed. The 1817-against-1822 repair is T-0893, and the John-Dean house itself — a five-room house at the foot of Randolph Street that this project models nothing of — is T-0895. NOTHING WAS RESIZED OR REGRADED ON THIS EVIDENCE: `bk_hub_063`'s two storeys against this record's inferred one is named in form.stories and left at one, for the reason written there. docs/RESEARCH/jb_beaubien_homestead.md § 6 is the full reading.
